title: My God, I love you (30 September 1897)
hookLine: after months of darkness, Thérèse's last words are plain ones
tomorrow: she never left her convent. so why is she patron of missions?

cards: Last words get quoted, framed, turned into captions. People expect them to be wise, or at least memorable. A gentle note for parents: today's story is about a death, told quietly.
Thérèse's last day is told by her sisters, in the account added at the end of The Story of a Soul. It is long and hard. She's in the convent infirmary, very sick, struggling to breathe.
Her sisters are gathered around the bed. She's holding a crucifix. Near the end, she looks at it, and she speaks.

teach.b: What she says, by her sisters' account, is: oh, I love him. And then: my God, I love you. Then she dies.

To hear why those words land, go back a few months. In Manuscript C, written near the end, Thérèse admits something her readers might not expect. The thought of heaven, once her joy, had become a fight.
She describes a darkness she couldn't see through, and says she kept choosing to believe anyway, and kept doing the small things.

She even says that when she wrote poems about heaven in those months, she was singing what she wanted to believe, not what she felt. So her last words don't come from a vision. No light breaks through in the account.
Pain, a crucifix, and a choice. Notice what she doesn't say. Not I see.

teach.h: NOT I SEE. NOT I FEEL. I LOVE.

teach.b: Jesus calls this the first commandment, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole mind."
Her last plain words answer it: not with her whole feeling, with her whole will.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the saint known for sweetness spent her last months in a darkness she described honestly, and still ended on love.
That's the little way at its smallest: one sentence, said to God, with nothing left to add.

how: Catholics keep a yearly feast for Thérèse, and some pray her last words as a short act of love.

s: Thérèse died peacefully, seeing heaven open before her
her sisters tell a hard last day, and she had written of a darkness about heaven she couldn't see through.
her last words were a short act of love
oh, I love him. my God, I love you.
Thérèse's trial of faith meant she stopped believing
she says she kept choosing to believe, in the dark.

games.q: your friend's grandfather is in hospice. she's scared she'll say the wrong thing on her last visit. what does Thérèse's last day suggest?
o: something short and true: I love you, thank you.
a long speech covering everything she never said.
nothing heavy; small talk, so he stays calm.
games.why: at the end, after months of darkness, Thérèse said it simply: my God, I love you. the plainest true words are enough.

practice: Close your eyes. If you pray, say her words once, quietly, as your own: my God, I love you. If not, say the name of someone you love, once, and stay with it while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: My God. The opening of her last line, said plainly, at the end of a long and dark trial.

orig.note: French, her own language, not Latin: my God, I love you, the last words her sisters recorded.

carryVoice: Keep this one: my god, I love you, simple enough to say tonight. Sleep in peace.
